parsed.summary: `compactnessCounterexample_bigO` proves the existence of a finite nonempty family F of connected, bipartite, non-acyclic graphs with two properties: a uniform c>0 with ex(n,F) ≥ c·n^{4/3} eventually for every F∈F, and ex(n,F) = O(n^{4/3−1/48}). It also derives that F is not compact and that the corrected Erdős–Simonovits compactness conjecture fails. `not_erdos_180` states the disproof of the conjecture directly. The most important caveat is `quantitativeCompactnessCounterexample`: it is quantified ∀ over all families and all c, C rather than ∃, so it asserts every family and every pair of reals satisfies the whole conjunction. That is literally false (for example family = ∅ or c = 0), so it is not a faithful rendering of Theorem 1.1. A kernel-checked proof of it would indicate a problem.

glossary.plain: A finite simple graph on vertex set Fin order.
The host on n vertices contains no member of the family as a (not necessarily induced) subgraph.
glossary.note: Uses Mathlib SimpleGraph.Free, i.e. not IsContained (injective homomorphism).

glossary.plain: ex(n,F): the maximum number of edges of an F-free graph on Fin n, with sup over the empty set = 0.
glossary.note: The empty graph on n vertices is F-free whenever F has no 0-vertex or edgeless member, so the sup is a true max.

glossary.plain: Every member of F contains a cycle.
glossary.standard_concept: family of graphs each containing a cycle

glossary.plain: There exist F∈F and C>0 with ex(n,F) ≤ C·ex(n,F) for all sufficiently large n.
Every finite nonempty family all of whose members contain cycles is compact.
For every F∈F, eventually c·n^{4/3} ≤ ex(n,F).
glossary.note: The constant c is uniform over the family; this is equivalent for a finite family (take the minimum).

lean_claims.plain: There is a finite nonempty family of graphs, each containing a cycle, that is not compact.

For EVERY finset of graphs F and EVERY reals c, C, all of the following hold. F is nonempty. Every member is connected, bipartite and contains a cycle. c>0 and C>0. Each member has ex ≥ c·n^{4/3} eventually. Every F-free host on n vertices has e^16 ≤ C·n^21. ex(n,F)^16 ≤ C·n^21 for all n. 1/48>0 and 21/16 = 4/3 − 1/48. F is not compact. The compactness conjecture fails.

There exist a finite nonempty family F of connected bipartite graphs each containing a cycle, and c>0, with three properties. Every F∈F has ex(n,F) ≥ c·n^{4/3} eventually. ex(n,F) = O(n^{4/3−1/48}) as n→∞. F is not compact. Hence the compactness conjecture is false.

paper_claims.plain: There exists a finite nonempty family F of connected bipartite graphs, each containing a cycle, with ex(n,F)=O(n^{4/3−1/48}) and ex(n,F)=Ω(n^{4/3}) for each F∈F. In particular no member satisfies (1), disproving the compactness conjecture.
There is a connected bipartite 2-degenerate H with ex(n,H) ≥ c·n^{3/2+ε} for all sufficiently large n.

coverage.why: Existential statement with matching hypotheses, the O-bound, the per-member Ω-bound and the non-compactness consequence.
Negation of the corrected compactness conjecture, matching (1).
Universally quantified over family, c and C instead of existentially, so the statement is false as written.

flags.explanation: The statement begins `∀ (family) (c C : ℝ)` and its body is a pure conjunction, so it claims every finset of graphs is nonempty, every c is positive, and so on. This is refutable: family = ∅ violates `family.Nonempty`, and c = 0 violates `0 < c`. The paper's claim is existential (∃ F, c, C). As written the theorem is false, so a kernel-accepted proof of it would signal an inconsistency or a mis-specified challenge. It does not formalize the paper's quantitative claim.
flags.probe_idea: theorem probe : ¬ (∀ (family : Finset FiniteGraph) (c C : ℝ), family.Nonempty ∧ ...) := fun h => by simpa using (h ∅ 1 1).1

flags.explanation: A single constant c is used for all members, whereas the paper's Ω implicitly allows constants depending on F. This is equivalent for finite families.

lint_verdicts.why: edgeFinset of a graph on Fin n is a genuine finite set; no infinite-type cardinality is involved.
Real division 4/3 of nonzero literals is the intended exponent.
Real arithmetic identity 21/16 = 4/3 − 1/48 is true and is not truncated.
Finite edge set card cast to ℝ; no junk value.
The real exponent 4/3 − 1/48 = 21/16 matches the paper.
